```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "A has no gating compliance cost before a first sale. B handles PHI, and its brief cites $8,000-$25,000 for a year-one HIPAA program plus BAAs, risk assessment and audited infrastructure. That cost and timeline is hard to fit into a one-person build aiming for revenue in 90 days.",
    "A's buyer path is documented for a solo seller. Several small competitors sell at $29-$149/mo, pitched as under the ~$10,000 micro-purchase threshold, which suggests some purchases avoid an RFP. That points to a self-serve close without enterprise sales, though the brief gives no conversion data.",
    "A's demand trigger is a sourced legal requirement, the DOJ Title II rule. The brief also includes an independent industry quote (Tyler Technologies) and NLC surveying cities on cost. B's demand evidence is anecdotal complaints about incumbent pricing, not a request for the proposed product.",
    "Both markets are crowded. A's competitors are mostly small and recent, so a new entrant could plausibly win a first customer. B's are entrenched, well-funded full EHRs already priced at $29-$99/mo, plus $8-10/mo reminder tools, which squeezes B's proposed $29-$69 price point.",
    "A has a cheap, concrete acquisition channel: municipal league booths at $1,300-$1,800 and sponsorships from $250. B's paid channel (Capterra) needs at least $500/mo, and its organic channel (r/therapists) is limited by self-promotion norms."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's claim of a 'documented segment' of price-sensitive solo therapists rests on two Reddit threads and a competitor's (Upheal/Oasys) marketing blog. The brief itself admits none of these complaints ask for a minimal notes+reminders app; they are about incumbent price and group-practice friction. Some B pricing is also weakly sourced: the SimplePractice $29 tier comes from unnamed 'third-party sources,' and TheraSoft and TheraFocus have no links. That leaves no direct evidence of demand for the proposed product.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate confidence. A has real weaknesses. The deadline extension to 2027/2028 weakens urgency. Six to seven near-identical scan tools suggest a price war. One key demand quote is vendor-sourced marketing copy, and the brief has no data on conversion from free scan to paid. A wins mainly because B faces a hard HIPAA cost and timeline barrier and has weaker demand evidence, not because A's own evidence is strong."
}
```
